title: The Experience Machine
summary:
Suppose, Robert Nozick wrote in 1974, there were an experience machine that could give you any experience you wanted: superduper neuropsychologists could stimulate your brain so that you would think and feel you were writing a great novel, or making a friend, or reading an interesting book, while all the time you were floating in a tank with electrodes attached to your brain. You could choose a lifetime of the best experiences. Would you plug in?

Most people say no, and Nozick took this to show that experience is not all that matters to us. We want to actually do things, not only to have the experience of doing them; we want to be a certain kind of person, not an indeterminate blob in a tank; and we want contact with a reality deeper than one someone has built. Hedonists reply that the refusal is just a bias towards what we already have: Felipe De Brigard (2010) told people their present life was already the machine, and most chose to stay plugged in.
citations: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (Basic Books, 1974), 42–45
Felipe De Brigard, "If You Like It, Does It Matter If It's Real?", Philosophical Psychology 23(1) (2010): 43–57
Andrew Moore, "Hedonism," Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/hedonism/
